meta.note: 'from' gives the id of the earlier body the tradition came out of, or null for churches that see themselves as continuous with the apostolic church. Each card describes the church as its own members do; see CREEDS_NOTES.md for points to check.
meta.holds_rule: held_by[].holds: formal (dogma, confession or liturgy), doctrine (teaching received; council not binding in itself), content (content affirmed, not binding), no, or unsettled. A church card's holds_creeds is every item whose row for that church is formal, doctrine or content.

churches.name: Catholic Church

began.display: Apostolic age (Catholics date the church to Christ and Pentecost, 1st century AD)

churches.where: Jerusalem, then Rome and the whole Roman world; centred on the see of Rome
churches.from_note: Sees itself as the church founded by Christ, with no parent body. Its Latin West and the Greek East parted in stages, with 1054 as the usual marker.
churches.why: Catholics believe Christ founded the church on the apostles, gave it the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and promised to stay with it to the end of time. They hold that this one church subsists in the Catholic Church, led by the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor with the bishops in communion with him. They also teach that real elements of grace and truth are found in other churches. Besides the Latin Church it includes Eastern Catholic churches with their own rites and laws.
key_people: Pope Leo I (his Tome was read at Chalcedon, 451)
Pope Gregory I (sent Augustine to England, 597)
Popes John XXIII and Paul VI (Vatican II)

key_events.event: Seven ecumenical councils, shared with the Orthodox.
Rome's legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople exchange excommunications; the estrangement of East and West deepens.
Council of Florence: a union with the Greek Church is agreed but not received in the East.
Council of Trent answers the Reformation.
Vatican I defines papal primacy and infallibility (18 July).
Second Vatican Council; ecumenical dialogue opens.
Joint declaration with Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I regrets the 1054 excommunications (7 December).
Common Christological Declaration with the Assyrian Church of the East.
Joint Declaration on Justification with the Lutheran World Federation.

churches.name: Eastern Orthodox Church
churches.where: The eastern Roman (Byzantine) world: Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem; later Slavic, Romanian, Georgian and other lands
churches.from_note: Sees itself as the unbroken continuation of the church of Christ and the apostles. Its separation from Rome grew from 1054 to a formal break in the 15th century.
churches.why: The Orthodox see their church as the same church founded by Christ and the apostles, keeping the faith of the seven ecumenical councils. It is a family of self-governing churches, with the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople as 'first among equals'. The split with Rome turned on the pope's claim to universal jurisdiction and on the Filioque added to the creed.

key_events.event: Seven ecumenical councils, the last being Nicaea II on icons.
Baptism of Kievan Rus'.
Rome's legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople exchange excommunications; the estrangement of East and West deepens.
The Fourth Crusade (sack of Constantinople, 1204) deepens the estrangement.
Formal break with Rome (WCC dates it to the 15th century; the union agreed at Florence in 1439 was not received in the East).
Patriarch Athenagoras I and Pope Paul VI regret the 1054 excommunications.

churches.name: Oriental Orthodox Churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Malankara/Indian)

began.display: Apostolic age; separate from the Chalcedonian churches after 451

churches.where: Egypt, Syria, Armenia, Ethiopia, Eritrea, India
churches.from_note: Founded in apostolic times by apostles or their first disciples (their own account, WCC). Not in communion with Rome or the Eastern Orthodox since the dispute over the Council of Chalcedon (451).
churches.why: These ancient churches keep the faith of the first three councils and follow Cyril of Alexandria's formula 'one nature of God the Word incarnate'. They did not accept Chalcedon's wording 'in two natures', which they read as dividing Christ. They call their teaching Miaphysite: one united nature of God the Word incarnate, fully God and fully human, without mixing or division. They are not Monophysite in the sense of Eutyches, whom they also reject.
key_people: Dioscorus of Alexandria (deposed at Chalcedon, honoured by these churches)

key_events.event: Council of Ephesus, the last council they accept.
Council of Chalcedon; these churches do not accept it, and the largest lasting division of the early church follows.
A separate line of Syriac Orthodox patriarchs takes shape.
Official theological dialogue with the Eastern Orthodox begins; Christological agreements follow.

churches.name: Church of the East (Assyrian Church of the East; Ancient Church of the East)

began.display: Earliest Christianity in Mesopotamia and Persia (1st-3rd century); organized as a church of the Persian Empire in 410

churches.where: Mesopotamia and the Persian (Sasanian) Empire; later Central Asia, China and South India; today Iraq, Iran, Syria and a large diaspora
churches.from_note: Traces its origins to the see of Seleucia-Ctesiphon and the apostle Thomas, with Addai and Mari (WCC). It grew outside the Roman Empire and its councils.
churches.why: Christians in the Persian Empire organized under their own Catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410 and received the faith of Nicaea. Following Theodore of Mopsuestia, they stress the full and distinct divinity and humanity of Christ; their theology took shape outside the councils of the Roman Empire. Opponents called them 'Nestorian', a name the church itself considers pejorative and scholars call misleading. It did not receive the Council of Ephesus (431) or later councils.

key_events.event: Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon under Catholicos Isaac officially receives the Council of Nicaea.
Synod of Markabta under Dadisho I ends appeals to 'Western' (Roman-Empire) bishops; sometimes read as a declaration of independence.
Synod under Acacius issues its first Christological statement after Ephesus and Chalcedon, in Antiochene terms.
The monk Aluoben reaches the Tang capital Chang'an (Xi'an) in 635; a stone monument set up there in 781 tells the story of the mission.
A separate patriarchal line in communion with Rome forms (Chaldean Catholic Church).
Division over adopting the Gregorian calendar and the hereditary succession of the patriarch; the Ancient Church of the East consecrates its own patriarch (1968).
Common Christological Declaration with the Catholic Church (11 November).

churches.name: Lutheran churches
churches.where: Wittenberg, Saxony; then much of Germany and Scandinavia
churches.from_note: A reform movement within the Western (Latin) Catholic Church that became separate churches.
churches.why: Martin Luther, a monk and professor, came to believe that sinners are made right with God by grace through faith in Christ, not by their own merit, and protested the sale of indulgences. When reform within the Roman church failed, evangelical princes and cities organized churches around the preached word, the sacraments and the Augsburg Confession.

key_events.event: Luther publishes his 95 Theses at Wittenberg; the usual start of the Reformation.
Excommunicated by Rome (January) and outlawed at the Diet of Worms (May); hidden at the Wartburg.
Luther's Small and Large Catechisms.
Augsburg Confession read before Charles V.
Death of Luther (18 February).
Book of Concord published.
Lutheran World Federation founded.
Joint Declaration on Justification with the Catholic Church.

churches.name: Reformed and Presbyterian churches
churches.where: Zurich and Geneva, Switzerland; then France, the Netherlands, the Palatinate, Scotland, Hungary and beyond
churches.from_note: Grew from the Swiss and French Reformation within the Western Catholic Church.
churches.why: Reformers such as Ulrich Zwingli in Zurich and John Calvin in Geneva sought to reform worship and doctrine strictly by Scripture, with Christ as the only head of the church. They stressed God's sovereign grace and governed churches through pastors and elders in local and regional assemblies. Presbyterians are the branch shaped in Scotland and England, chiefly by John Knox and the Westminster Assembly.

key_events.event: Zwingli begins preaching reform in Zurich.
Calvin is held in Geneva by William Farel; he settles there for good in 1541.
Scots Confession and the Scottish Reformation under John Knox (First Book of Discipline).
Belgic Confession and Heidelberg Catechism.
Synod of Dort.
Westminster Confession; adopted in Scotland 1647.
World Communion of Reformed Churches associates with the Joint Declaration on Justification.

churches.name: Anglican Communion (Church of England, Episcopal Church and others)

began.display: English church from 597 (and earlier British Christianity); separate from Rome 1534; settled identity under Elizabeth I from 1558/1559

churches.where: England; then Ireland, Scotland, the United States and worldwide
churches.from_note: The English church, part of the Western Catholic Church since the 597 mission and earlier Celtic and British streams, broke with papal authority under Henry VIII.
churches.why: Anglicans see their church as the ancient Catholic church of England, reformed in the 16th century. The break with Rome came when the pope refused to annul Henry VIII's marriage and English rulers claimed authority over the English church; reform deepened under Edward VI and was settled under Elizabeth I. It keeps bishops, the Book of Common Prayer and continuity with the early church, while holding Reformation teaching.

key_events.event: Mission from Pope Gregory the Great under Augustine lands in Kent.
Synod of Whitby joins the Roman and Celtic streams.
Act of Supremacy names the king supreme head of the Church of England.
First Book of Common Prayer (Cranmer); its 1662 revision is still standard in England.

churches.name: Methodist churches (including the Holiness movement)

began.display: 1729-1739 (Oxford group 1729; movement from 1739); separate church in America 1784

churches.where: Oxford and Bristol/London, England; then America (Baltimore, 1784) and worldwide
churches.from_note: A revival movement inside the Church of England that became separate churches. The Holiness churches grew out of American Methodism in the 19th century.
churches.why: John and Charles Wesley sought to bring warmer faith and disciplined holiness to the Church of England. They taught that God's grace is offered to all, that faith changes character, and that perfect love is possible in this life. Their societies outgrew the established church, first in America after independence and later in Britain. The Holiness movement set out to recover Wesley's teaching on entire sanctification.

key_events.event: John Wesley joins the Oxford student group led by Charles.

Methodism as a movement begins.
Methodist Episcopal Church organized at Baltimore; Articles of Religion adopted; Asbury and Coke as superintendents (called bishops from the late 1780s).
Plan of Pacification lets British Methodist chapels give the sacraments.
African Methodist Episcopal Church organized (Richard Allen).

Church of the Nazarene (Holiness).
United Methodist Church formed.
World Methodist Council associates with the Joint Declaration on Justification.

churches.name: Baptist churches

began.display: 1609 (Amsterdam); first Baptist church in England 1611 or 1612

churches.where: Amsterdam, then London; later America and worldwide
churches.from_note: English Separatists who had left the Church of England (John Smyth's congregation from Gainsborough).
churches.why: John Smyth's exiled English congregation in Amsterdam concluded from the New Testament that the church is a fellowship of believers, so baptism should follow a personal confession of faith rather than be given to infants. Thomas Helwys led part of the group back to London and pleaded for religious freedom for all. Baptists hold the Bible as their only binding authority and give each local church freedom to order its life.

key_events.event: Smyth's congregation in Amsterdam adopts believers' baptism.
Helwys founds the first Baptist church in England, in London.
Roger Williams founds the first Baptist church in America, at Providence.
Seven Particular Baptist churches in London issue the First London Confession; General Baptist churches number about 47.
Second London Confession.
Philadelphia Baptist Association adopts the confession.
General and Particular Baptists unite in the Baptist Union of Great Britain and Ireland.
Baptist World Alliance founded.

Only the 1689 Confession is in creeds.json; many Baptists use other confessions. One historic exception: the General Baptist Orthodox Creed (drafted 1678, printed 1679) received the Nicene, Athanasian and Apostles' Creeds.

churches.name: Anabaptist churches (Mennonite, Amish, Hutterite; the Church of the Brethren shares this heritage)
churches.where: Zurich, Switzerland; then South Germany, Moravia and the Netherlands
churches.from_note: Began among Zwingli's followers in Zurich, in what historians call the Radical Reformation.
churches.why: A circle of Zwingli's followers believed Scripture required faster change, above all baptism only for those who confess faith and choose to follow Jesus. On 21 January 1525 they baptized one another in Zurich and formed free churches of committed believers, separate from the state, who refused the sword and the oath. Despite fierce persecution they spread, and Menno Simons gathered the Dutch and North German groups later called Mennonites.

key_events.event: First believers' baptisms in Felix Manz's house, Zurich.
Schleitheim Confession.
Jakob Hutter comes to lead the Moravian communities later called Hutterites.
Menno Simons joins the Anabaptists.
Dordrecht Confession.
Amish division among the Swiss Brethren.
Mennonite World Conference begins.

churches.name: Pentecostal and Charismatic churches

began.display: 1901-1906 (Topeka 1 January 1901; Azusa Street, Los Angeles, April 1906); Charismatic renewal from 1960

churches.where: Topeka, Kansas, and Los Angeles, California; spread worldwide within a few years; also independent beginnings in India (1905-1906), Korea (1907) and Chile (1909)
churches.from_note: Mainly from the Wesleyan Holiness movement, with others from Reformed and Keswick circles. The later Charismatic renewal stayed inside historic churches (Episcopal 1960, Catholic 1967).
churches.why: Believers seeking more of God's power prayed for a fresh Pentecost and began to speak in tongues. Many took this as the Bible evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:4). They saw this as restoring the gifts of the apostolic church for holy living and worldwide mission. From the 1960s many in older churches had the same experience and stayed in their own churches as Charismatics.

key_events.event: Students at Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka speak in tongues.
Azusa Street Mission revival under William J. Seymour begins (to 1909).
Assemblies of God organized at Hot Springs, Arkansas.
AG Statement of Fundamental Truths; Oneness ministers, who hold one God revealed as Father, Son and Spirit, leave.
Dennis Bennett's resignation at St Mark's Episcopal, Van Nuys, brings national attention to the Charismatic movement.
Catholic Charismatic Renewal begins at a Duquesne University retreat.
